A standard file describing how a chip's pins behave in a circuit. Somebody else can then simulate a board without being shown what is inside the chip.
A small shoulder-fired weapon, in between a pistol and a rifle. Here it shares its cartridge with the pistol, which is the point of the shared parts list.

The hard grain a carbide cutting tool is made of. On its own it is brittle, so it is bonded together with a softer metal — the Co in WC-Co.
The oldest light there is, left over from when the universe first went clear. It is the furthest thing anyone can see, which is why it turns up here.

The standard model of an expanding universe, named after the four people who wrote it down. The essay defends it rather than attacking it.
The research group whose published mouse result is cited here: a gene therapy that added about a fifth to male-mouse lifespan. Cited as real, not claimed.

An agreed table of how thick the air is at each height. Two people working out a bullet's flight then start from the same air, so the answers can be compared.
The armour rating everyone quotes. The two points the model is anchored to are one that stops a pistol round and one that stops a rifle round.
The standard explosive, and the one everything else gets compared against. Here it is a mixture being described on paper, not a thing being built.
One of the old text-prediction methods, from before neural networks. It guesses the next letter from the last few, which is the ceiling this work aims to break.

A way of quoting how much raw work a chip gets through each second. Easy to print on a slide; the audit here could not check it without the hardware.

A random answer that comes with a proof it was not rigged. Anyone can check the proof, and nobody gets to choose the answer.

Small enough to go in through a vein, on a drip, rather than needing surgery. On this page that is an assumption, not something anyone has shown.
Steady current that does not wiggle at all. At the bottom of a frequency range it means zero, so the band starts from nothing and goes up.
The paper's own name for the single idea underneath its three results. Keep nudging a guess along a little at a time, on a curved space rather than a flat one.
The program on this site that hides who is talking to whom. Encryption hides what you said; this hides that you spoke at all.
Two things on this site. The encryption scheme that works out its own one-time number instead of sending it. And ARIA-INTEL, the tracking prototype behind SENTINEL.
The crime-analysis program on this site. It reads public crime data and ranks where to look next. Every lead traces back to the record it came from.
The short name for ParanoidBSD, the operating system built here. It moves a hardened BSD system to C++23 and gives each program only the access it needs.
The short name for HardenedBSD on these pages. ParanoidBSD keeps its hardening and builds the new security model on top of it.
Two different things here. In the compression work: a way of scoring a trained network by how hard it squeezes data. In the drug work: a solvent that sets a gel once it meets water.
One of three compression frameworks here. It puts perfect and lossy squeezing on one sliding scale instead of treating them as two separate kinds of thing.
Energy-Resource Economic Model. It measures what a country is worth in units of energy instead of money, so the figure does not rest on trusting a bank.
Total National Wealth. The single number in that energy model: a country's energy, factories, food, water and people, all added up in one physical unit.
The main American share index. The paper counts how many bets are placed on it, 867 times more than in 1999, and asks where that ends.
A whole invented country, worked out on paper: government, money, defence, drugs, foreign policy. The point is that the parts must not contradict each other.
General Purpose Networks. One of the invented AI families in the fictional-country folder, written up with real theorem statements although the systems do not exist.
Torpedo Data Computer. The US Navy's 1932 aiming machine for submarines, rebuilt here as software and measured, including the drag and momentum of its own gears.
A design where the optimiser, the scheduler and the memory turn out to be one trick. One piece of machinery, doing every job.
Universal Statistical Generator. A text generator that counts patterns instead of training a network, using a fixed-size table so long context stops costing so much.
Unified Hash-Predictive Memory. It looks things up and works things out with one set of sums, rather than bolting memory onto a model afterwards.
Verification-Enabled Reasoning and Integrated Theorem-Acquiring System. It checks that each learning step is allowed before taking it, rather than proving afterwards that it was.
A way of recognising things, copied from the immune system. The body builds defences against germs it has never met by mixing a small set of parts.
Logarithmic Complexity Reduction Principle. The claim that the many places where a slow method becomes a fast one are all the same few tricks, not separate luck.
Quantum Graph Optimisation. A pipeline that pretends to be a quantum computer on an ordinary one, and treats the noise as useful information rather than a nuisance.
The gravity theory on the physics shelf. It lets gravity reach across distance in a new way while still never sending a signal faster than light.
A way of joining two pieces of metal without melting them. Heat, electricity and sound work together in a chemical bath, instead of a costly vacuum chamber.
The prefix naming the five settings of that metal-joining process. ULTRA-FLASH is two minutes at 150 °C; ULTRA-PRECISION takes half an hour or more, hotter.
The cutting-tool design on the shelf: a carbide tip that changes composition through its thickness, aimed at hard metals where ordinary tools give out.
A thought experiment about building a quantum computer out of flaws in diamond that work at room temperature. Most of the paper is the seven reasons it cannot be done yet.
Neural Quantum Dust. Tiny diamond specks injected into the blood to listen to single brain cells, read by dust-sized chips powered by ultrasound from outside.
A written-out plan for changing human genes to raise what a body can do. It is labelled speculation, and it publishes its own guess at the harm: 20 to 32 percent.
Three of the four genes that can wind a grown cell back towards a younger state. The fourth is left out on purpose.
A real published trial of the drug rapamycin. The human-enhancement paper cites it as a genuine result, to separate what is real from what it is only imagining.
An invented drug in the medicines folder, written up with a full made-up file. Every invented compound there carries a banner saying it is fiction.
The body-armour system in the police and defence folders. The police version is specified at 6.5 kg against the 20.25 kg gear it would replace.
One of four random-number generators on the shelf. It uses old, well-understood arithmetic at a very large size, and is the one put through the standard test battery.
Quality control. Checking the work as it is being done, rather than finding out at the end that a whole batch is wrong.
Central bank digital currency: money issued by a country's central bank in electronic form, rather than as notes and coins. Many countries are now working on one.
Cold dark matter, the standard picture of what the universe is mostly made of. ΛCDM is that picture plus the force pushing the universe apart.
A proposed change to the rule limiting how precisely you can pin down a particle. The paper notes it could clash with very fine measurements unless the effect is tiny.
The usual way a group of computers agrees on something when some of them may lie or fail. It works, but everybody has to message everybody.
Several parties working out an answer together without any of them revealing what they put in. Each learns the result and nothing else.
A function that turns any input into output nobody can tell from random, unless they hold the key. Much of modern encryption is built on one.
Using a cipher by numbering the blocks and scrambling the numbers, so you can jump straight to any part without working through the rest.
The common way of using AES so it both scrambles a message and catches tampering. It needs a number used once, and breaks badly if that number repeats.
Information-set decoding, the best known way of attacking codes like the one this scheme leans on. Its cost is what the security claim is measured against.
The property that nobody can forge a new valid message tag. The page says this scheme has no proof of it yet, which is the honest thing to say.
The fair test for a forging attack. The attacker is first allowed to ask for tags on any messages they like, then has to forge a new one.
Writing a yes-or-no rule as nothing but ANDs and exclusive-ORs. Every such rule has exactly one form like this, which makes two of them easy to compare.
Short for a finite field: arithmetic with only a fixed, finite set of numbers, where results wrap around instead of running off. GF(2) has just 0 and 1.
A set of points joined by one-way arrows, with no way to follow the arrows in a circle. Useful whenever one thing must happen before another.
One of the oldest ways of making random-looking numbers: multiply, add, keep the remainder, repeat. Fast and simple, and not random enough on its own.
A random number generator. A machine or piece of code that produces numbers with no pattern anyone can find, which much of security rests on.
A recipe for solving hard choosing problems on a quantum computer. Here it is only simulated on an ordinary machine, and no advantage is claimed.
A fast way of breaking a signal into the simple waves that make it up. It is one of the most used pieces of maths in computing.
The library most people reach for when they need that wave-splitting done fast. Named here as the kind of tuned code these results were not compared against.
Exploring a network by taking every step one hop from where you are before going any deeper. It finds the shortest route first.
Exploring a network by following one path as far as it goes, then backing up and trying the next. Uses far less memory than the alternative.
The standard way of guessing where something is from noisy readings. It keeps one running best guess and nudges it as each new reading arrives.
Several different guesses about how a thing is moving, all running at once. The evidence decides which one to believe right now.
Deciding which sighting belongs to which tracked thing. It weighs every possible pairing at once rather than committing to one and being wrong.
The score used to mark a tracker's work. It rolls missed things, invented things and how far off the positions were into one number you can compare.
The part of the tracker that measures its own noise while it runs. How jumpy the sensor is, and how jumpy the movement is, instead of being told up front.
A check on whether a run of numbers still resembles itself a few steps later. If it does when it should not, something has gone wrong.
The usual way of saying how far off a set of guesses was, on average. Big misses count for more than small ones, on purpose.
A single number saying which of two answers the evidence favours, and by how much. Positive one way, negative the other, zero for no idea.
A running average that quietly forgets the past: each new number counts a little, and everything older fades. Cheap, and it never has to store the history.
A way of measuring how alike two things are that only cares how far apart they sit. Similar things score high, distant things score near zero.
A way of hashing that puts similar things in the same bucket on purpose. It is how you find the nearest match without comparing against everything.
A model of something that moves through hidden states you cannot see directly, where each state leaves clues. Speech and handwriting were done this way for years.
Short for neural network. Layers of simple sums stacked up, where the stack as a whole does something useful and no single layer does much.
The plainest kind of neural network: layers where every unit feeds every unit in the next layer, and nothing loops back.
A kind of neural network with a memory it can choose to keep or wipe, built for sequences. It was the standard before attention took over.
Two networks trained against each other: one makes fakes, the other tries to spot them. Both get better until the fakes are hard to tell apart.
A version of that two-network setup with a different scoring rule, meant to stop training collapsing. It was tried here against AES, and still failed.
The usual score for a yes-or-no answer. It punishes a model harder the more confident it was when it got the answer wrong.
One of the small bending functions placed between layers of a network. Without one, a stack of layers would collapse into a single straight-line sum.
How most models are trained: look at a small batch, nudge the settings a little in the direction that helps, repeat millions of times.
Training something that reads a sequence by unrolling it into one long chain. The blame for the final answer is then traced back through every step.
A plan for how fast a model learns during training. Warm up, hold steady for most of the run, then slow down at the end.
Data that looks nothing like anything the model was trained on. Its answers there stop meaning much, and it will usually not admit that.
A tidier version of the random-features trick, where the random directions are spread out evenly rather than drawn at random. Building it here found a real bug.
A way of promising a learner will probably be roughly right. It says how many examples you need before the odds of being badly wrong are small.
Algorithmic learning theory. It counts how many mistakes a learner can make before it settles down, rather than how much data it needs.
Getting software to handle written language. On this site it means the old rule-based kind, chosen because a police tool has to be able to explain itself.
